question: What is the punishment for murder under current Indian law?
expected_answer: Murder is punishable under Section 103(1) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 with death or imprisonment for life, plus fine.

question: Does Indian law now have a specific provision for mob lynching?
expected_answer: Yes. Section 103(2) BNS specifically punishes murder by a group of five or more persons on grounds like race, caste, community, sex, language or personal belief, with death or life imprisonment and fine.
required_facts: ground of race, caste or community

question: Is sedition still a crime in India after the new criminal laws?
expected_answer: The IPC sedition offence (Section 124A) was not retained. BNS Section 152 instead punishes acts endangering the sovereignty, unity and integrity of India, with imprisonment for life or up to 7 years plus fine. Criticism of the government without inciting such acts is not covered.
forbidden_facts: sedition under 124A is still in force

question: Which section of the new criminal code covers cheating?
expected_answer: Cheating is covered by Section 318 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023. Where the victim is dishonestly induced to deliver property, Section 318(4) prescribes imprisonment up to 7 years plus fine.

question: Someone posing as a bank officer tricked my father into transferring Rs 2 lakh. What offences does this involve?
expected_answer: This is cheating by personation and dishonest inducement to deliver property under Section 318(4) BNS, and cheating by personation using a computer resource under Section 66D of the IT Act. Report immediately on the 1930 cyber fraud helpline and cybercrime.gov.in, and file an FIR.

question: Is chain snatching treated differently from ordinary theft now?
expected_answer: Yes. The BNS created a separate offence of snatching in Section 304 — sudden, quick or forcible seizure of movable property from a person — punishable with imprisonment up to 3 years and fine, distinct from ordinary theft under Section 303.

question: What punishment does a first-time offender face for stealing something worth less than Rs 5,000?
expected_answer: For theft of property under Rs 5,000, a first-time offender who returns or restores the property can be punished with community service under the proviso to Section 303(2) BNS, instead of jail.

question: What is community service as a punishment in Indian criminal law?
expected_answer: Community service is a new form of punishment introduced by the BNS for petty offences — such as small first-time theft after returning the property, defamation, public misconduct by a drunk person, and attempt to commit suicide to restrain a public servant — where the court orders unpaid work of public utility instead of imprisonment.

question: A speeding car hit and killed a pedestrian, and the driver stopped and reported it to police. What is the maximum punishment?
expected_answer: Causing death by rash or negligent driving, where the driver reports the incident, is punishable under Section 106(1) BNS with imprisonment up to 5 years and fine. It is not murder because there was no intention to kill.

question: Is the 10-year jail provision for hit-and-run drivers currently in force?
expected_answer: No. Section 106(2) BNS — up to 10 years for fleeing an accident without reporting — was deferred after nationwide transporter protests and has not been brought into force. Section 106(1) (up to 5 years) is in force.

question: What is 'organised crime' under the new criminal law?
expected_answer: Section 111 BNS, for the first time in the general criminal code, punishes organised crime — continuing unlawful activity like kidnapping, extortion, land grabbing, contract killing, cyber-crime or trafficking, carried out by groups or syndicates for material benefit. If it results in death, punishment can extend to death or life imprisonment.
required_facts: continuing unlawful activity by a syndicate

question: What is 'petty organised crime'?
expected_answer: Section 112 BNS punishes petty organised crime — organised vehicle theft, pickpocketing, snatching, theft in public transport and similar acts committed by groups — with imprisonment of one to seven years and fine.
required_facts: organised petty theft or snatching by groups

question: Are terrorist acts now covered by the general criminal code?
expected_answer: Yes. Section 113 BNS brings terrorist acts into the general criminal code for the first time (previously they were mainly under the UAPA). It covers acts intended to threaten India's unity, integrity, sovereignty, security or economic security or to strike terror, with punishments up to death or life imprisonment.

question: A man had a sexual relationship with a woman by promising marriage he never intended. Is this an offence?
expected_answer: Yes. Section 69 BNS punishes sexual intercourse obtained by deceitful means — including a false promise of marriage made without intention to fulfil it, or false promise of employment or promotion — with imprisonment up to 10 years and fine. Courts require the promise to have been false from the beginning.

question: My in-laws harass me daily for dowry. Which criminal provision protects me?
expected_answer: Cruelty by a husband or his relatives is an offence under Section 85 BNS, punishable with imprisonment up to 3 years and fine. You can file an FIR, and also seek civil protection orders under the Domestic Violence Act, 2005. Demanding dowry is separately punishable under the Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961.

question: What is a dowry death and its punishment under current law?
expected_answer: Under Section 80 BNS, if a woman dies of burns or unnatural causes within 7 years of marriage and she faced dowry-related cruelty or harassment soon before death, it is dowry death, punishable with imprisonment of at least 7 years, extendable to life.

question: What is the minimum punishment for rape under the BNS?
expected_answer: Rape is punishable under Section 64 BNS with rigorous imprisonment of not less than 10 years, extendable to life imprisonment, plus fine.

question: What punishment does gang rape attract under current law?
expected_answer: Gang rape is punishable under Section 70 BNS with rigorous imprisonment of at least 20 years, extendable to life. Where the victim is a woman under 18, Section 70(2) provides life imprisonment for the remainder of natural life or death.

question: A colleague keeps making sexually coloured remarks despite my objections. Is this a criminal offence?
expected_answer: Yes. Sexually coloured remarks and unwelcome sexual advances are sexual harassment under Section 75 BNS, punishable with imprisonment up to 3 years or fine or both. At a workplace, you can also complain to the Internal Committee under the POSH Act, 2013.

question: Someone secretly filmed a woman in a changing room. What offence is this?
expected_answer: Watching or capturing images of a woman engaged in a private act is voyeurism under Section 77 BNS (first conviction 1-3 years). Sharing such images also attracts Section 66E of the IT Act and, for obscene content, Section 67.

question: A man follows me home from work every day and messages me constantly despite my clear refusal. What can I do legally?
expected_answer: This is stalking under Section 78 BNS — following a woman or monitoring her despite clear disinterest — punishable up to 3 years for the first conviction and 5 years for repeat offences. File an FIR at any police station; online stalking is equally covered.

question: Which BNS section punishes assault on a woman with intent to outrage her modesty?
expected_answer: Section 74 BNS punishes assault or criminal force against a woman with intent to outrage her modesty, with imprisonment of 1 to 5 years plus fine.

question: Is making obscene gestures or remarks at a woman on the street an offence?
expected_answer: Yes. Any word, sound, gesture or object intended to insult the modesty of a woman is punishable under Section 79 BNS with simple imprisonment up to 3 years plus fine.

question: What is the punishment for attempt to murder?
expected_answer: Attempt to murder is punishable under Section 109 BNS with imprisonment up to 10 years and fine; if hurt is caused in the attempt, punishment can extend to imprisonment for life.

question: My neighbour slapped me during an argument. What offence is this and what is the punishment?
expected_answer: Voluntarily causing hurt is punishable under Section 115(2) BNS with imprisonment up to 1 year or fine up to Rs 10,000 or both. You can file a complaint or FIR; simple hurt cases are also compoundable (can be settled).

question: What is the difference between hurt and grievous hurt?
expected_answer: Hurt is causing bodily pain, disease or infirmity. Grievous hurt covers specified serious injuries — emasculation, permanent loss of sight or hearing, fracture, permanent disfigurement, or injury causing severe pain or inability to follow ordinary pursuits for 20 days — and attracts higher punishment under the BNS.
required_facts: grievous hurt includes fracture and permanent damage

question: Which provision covers kidnapping under the new criminal code?
expected_answer: Kidnapping is covered by Section 137 BNS — kidnapping from India or from lawful guardianship — punishable with imprisonment up to 7 years and fine.

question: Someone is threatening to kill me over a property dispute. What offence is this?
expected_answer: Criminal intimidation is punishable under Section 351 BNS — up to 2 years for simple threats, and up to 7 years where the threat is of death or grievous hurt. File an FIR; preserve messages or recordings as evidence.

question: Can I be jailed for defaming someone on social media?
expected_answer: Yes. Defamation is punishable under Section 356 BNS with simple imprisonment up to 2 years, or fine, or both, or community service. Truth for public good, fair comment and other exceptions apply. The defamed person can also sue for civil damages.
required_facts: community service is a possible punishment

question: My business partner refuses to return money I entrusted to him for a specific purpose and has used it himself. What offence is this?
expected_answer: Dishonest misappropriation of property entrusted to someone is criminal breach of trust under Section 316 BNS, punishable with imprisonment and fine. You can file an FIR and also pursue civil recovery. Note that a purely commercial non-payment without dishonesty is a civil dispute, not a crime.

question: What is the punishment for robbery?
expected_answer: Robbery — theft or extortion with violence or fear of instant harm — is punishable under Section 309 BNS with rigorous imprisonment up to 10 years and fine.

question: What does 'common intention' mean in criminal law?
expected_answer: When a criminal act is done by several persons in furtherance of a common intention, each person is liable as if he did the act alone. This principle, formerly IPC Section 34, is now Section 3(5) of the BNS.

question: Can a 6-year-old child be prosecuted for a crime?
expected_answer: No. Nothing done by a child under 7 years of age is an offence (Section 20 BNS). For children between 7 and 12, liability depends on maturity of understanding. Older children are dealt with under the Juvenile Justice Act, not ordinary criminal courts.
required_facts: child under 7 cannot commit an offence

question: If someone attacks me, how much force can I legally use to defend myself?
expected_answer: Every person has a right of private defence of body and property under the BNS. The force must be proportionate to the threat, and can extend even to causing death where there is reasonable apprehension of death, grievous hurt, rape, kidnapping or similar grave offences. The right lasts only while the threat continues.
required_facts: can extend to causing death for grave threats

question: Is attempting suicide a crime in India now?
expected_answer: The general offence of attempted suicide (old IPC 309) was not retained in the BNS, and the Mental Healthcare Act, 2017 presumes a person attempting suicide is under severe stress and bars prosecution. Only attempting suicide to compel or restrain a public servant remains punishable (Section 226 BNS).

question: Is adultery a criminal offence in India?
expected_answer: No. The Supreme Court struck down the adultery offence in Joseph Shine v. Union of India (2018), and the BNS does not criminalise adultery. It remains a ground for divorce in matrimonial law.

question: What is criminal conspiracy under the BNS?
expected_answer: Criminal conspiracy — an agreement between two or more persons to do an illegal act or a legal act by illegal means — is punishable under Section 61 BNS (formerly IPC 120A/120B).
required_facts: agreement between two or more persons

question: Which provision punishes promoting enmity between religious groups?
expected_answer: Section 196 BNS punishes promoting enmity between groups on grounds of religion, race, place of birth, residence or language and acts prejudicial to harmony (formerly IPC 153A).

question: What is extortion and how is it different from theft?
expected_answer: Extortion (Section 308 BNS) is intentionally putting a person in fear of injury to dishonestly obtain property or valuables from them — the victim delivers the property under fear. In theft (Section 303 BNS), property is taken without consent, not delivered.
required_facts: delivery under fear vs taking without consent

question: When did the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita replace the Indian Penal Code?
expected_answer: The BNS, 2023 came into force on 1 July 2024, replacing the Indian Penal Code, 1860. Offences committed before that date are still tried under the IPC.
required_facts: offences before that date under IPC

question: How many sections does the BNS have compared to the IPC?
expected_answer: The BNS has 358 sections, down from 511 sections in the IPC, with completely reorganised numbering — no major IPC section keeps the same number in the BNS.

question: What is culpable homicide and how is it different from murder?
expected_answer: Culpable homicide is causing death by an act done with the intention or knowledge that it may cause death. Murder is the aggravated form — with intention to kill or knowledge of near-certain death — and carries death or life imprisonment. Culpable homicide not amounting to murder covers less aggravated cases (e.g. sudden provocation) with lesser punishment.

question: During a sudden quarrel my brother hit a man who died. Is this necessarily murder?
expected_answer: Not necessarily. Death caused without premeditation in a sudden fight in the heat of passion may be culpable homicide not amounting to murder, which carries lesser punishment than murder. The exact charge depends on intention, weapon and circumstances — engage a criminal lawyer immediately.
required_facts: culpable homicide not amounting to murder

question: What does 'abetment' mean in criminal law?
expected_answer: Abetment means instigating a person to commit an offence, engaging in a conspiracy for it, or intentionally aiding its commission. An abettor can be punished even if the main offence is committed by someone else.

question: A mob of six people beat a man to death over suspected cattle theft, targeting him because of his community. What charge applies?
expected_answer: Murder by a group of 5 or more persons on the ground of community is specifically punishable under Section 103(2) BNS with death or life imprisonment and fine — the mob-lynching provision introduced in 2024. Each member of the group is liable.

question: Gang members demand monthly 'protection money' from my shop, threatening damage if I refuse. What offences apply?
expected_answer: Demanding money under threat is extortion (Section 308 BNS); done as continuing unlawful activity by a gang or syndicate, it can amount to organised crime under Section 111 BNS with much harsher punishment. File an FIR — police protection can be sought.

question: A fake astrologer took Rs 50,000 from my mother promising to cure my father's illness. Is this a crime?
expected_answer: Yes. Dishonestly inducing a person to deliver money by deception is cheating under Section 318 BNS — inducement to deliver property attracts up to 7 years under Section 318(4). File an FIR with evidence of payment and the false promises.

question: What is the punishment for sexual harassment under the BNS?
expected_answer: Sexual harassment — physical contact with unwelcome sexual overtures, demands for sexual favours, showing pornography against a woman's will, or sexually coloured remarks — is punishable under Section 75 BNS with imprisonment up to 3 years or fine or both.

question: Someone morphed my sister's photo obscenely and is threatening to post it unless she pays. What offences are involved?
expected_answer: This involves extortion (Section 308 BNS), and publishing obscene electronic material would attract Section 67 IT Act; violation-of-privacy imaging attracts Section 66E IT Act. Report on cybercrime.gov.in or the 1930 helpline immediately and preserve all messages — do not pay.

question: Which BNS provision replaced IPC Section 302, and does the section number 302 mean anything in the BNS?
expected_answer: Murder (old IPC 302) is now Section 103 BNS. The number 302 in the BNS belongs to a completely different offence — the renumbering means old section numbers must never be assumed to carry over.

question: What is 'rioting' in Indian criminal law?
expected_answer: When force or violence is used by an unlawful assembly (five or more persons with a common illegal object), every member is guilty of rioting, punishable under the BNS with imprisonment and fine — more severely if armed with deadly weapons.
required_facts: unlawful assembly of five or more

question: My tenant refuses to vacate and has stopped paying rent. Can I file a criminal case for trespass?
expected_answer: Generally no. A tenant who entered lawfully and overstays is a civil matter — eviction must go through the rent court/civil court under the state rent law. Criminal trespass requires entry with intent to commit an offence or intimidate. Forcibly evicting the tenant yourself is illegal.
required_facts: overstaying tenant is a civil matter

question: What happens if someone files a deliberately false FIR against me?
expected_answer: Filing false information with police and fabricating false evidence are themselves offences under the BNS, and malicious prosecution can ground civil damages. You can seek quashing of the false FIR in the High Court and anticipatory bail if arrest is feared. Keep evidence disproving the allegation.
required_facts: false information to police is an offence

question: Are men protected against sexual offences under the BNS?
expected_answer: Partially. BNS rape provisions protect women only, and the old IPC 377 (which covered non-consensual acts against men) was not retained in the BNS — a gap widely noted. Non-consensual acts against men can still be prosecuted as hurt, wrongful restraint or other general offences; children of all genders are protected by POCSO.

question: What is 'wrongful restraint' versus 'wrongful confinement'?
expected_answer: Wrongful restraint is obstructing a person from proceeding in a direction they have a right to go; wrongful confinement is the graver form — restraining a person within circumscribing limits so they cannot leave at all. Both are offences under the BNS.

question: An online seller took full payment and never shipped, and now ignores all messages. Criminal or civil?
expected_answer: If there was dishonest intention from the start — fake listing, disappearing after payment — it is cheating under Section 318 BNS and can be reported at cybercrime.gov.in or via FIR. A genuine transaction gone wrong is a consumer dispute — file before the Consumer Commission instead.

question: What does 'cognizable offence' mean?
expected_answer: A cognizable offence is one in which police can register an FIR and arrest without a warrant — generally the more serious offences like murder, rape, robbery and cheating. For non-cognizable offences, police need a Magistrate's order to investigate.

question: What is a 'bailable' versus 'non-bailable' offence?
expected_answer: In a bailable offence, bail is a right — police or court must release the accused on bail. In a non-bailable offence, bail is not automatic; it is granted at the court's discretion considering the gravity of the offence, flight risk and possibility of tampering with evidence.

question: What is a 'compoundable' offence?
expected_answer: A compoundable offence is one the victim can lawfully settle with the accused, ending the prosecution — typically minor offences like simple hurt or defamation. Serious offences are non-compoundable, though High Courts can quash some cases on genuine settlement.

question: My domestic worker was caught stealing Rs 2,000, admitted it and returned the money. Will she go to jail?
expected_answer: Not necessarily. Theft under Rs 5,000 by a first-time offender, where the property is returned, can be punished with community service under the proviso to Section 303(2) BNS. Theft is also compoundable in specified circumstances, so a settlement is possible.
required_facts: community service for petty first-time theft

question: A drunk man was creating a scene and abusing passers-by in the market. What does the law provide?
expected_answer: Public misconduct by a drunk person is a petty offence under the BNS for which the court can now order community service instead of jail. Aggressive acts like assault or intimidation are charged separately.

question: Does the BNS apply to offences committed before 1 July 2024?
expected_answer: No. Offences committed before 1 July 2024 continue to be investigated and tried under the IPC, and Article 20(1) of the Constitution bars retrospective criminal punishment. The BNS applies to offences committed on or after that date.
required_facts: IPC applies to pre-1 July 2024 offences

question: What is 'organised crime' punishment if it results in someone's death?
expected_answer: Under Section 111 BNS, if organised crime results in death, the punishment is death or imprisonment for life, plus a substantial fine; other cases attract imprisonment of at least 5 years extendable to life.
required_facts: death or life imprisonment if death results

question: I received counterfeit currency from a shop. Who is liable?
expected_answer: Knowingly using or trafficking counterfeit currency is a serious BNS offence; innocently receiving a fake note is not. Hand the note to police or your bank with details of where you got it — attempting to pass it on after knowing it is fake becomes an offence.

question: The BNS punishes 'snatching' — what exactly must the prosecution show?
expected_answer: Under Section 304 BNS, snatching is theft where the offender suddenly, quickly or forcibly seizes, grabs or takes away movable property from a person or their possession — e.g. chain or phone snatching. It carries imprisonment up to 3 years plus fine.
required_facts: sudden or forcible seizure from the person

question: Can a woman be prosecuted for cruelty under Section 85 BNS?
expected_answer: Yes. Section 85 BNS punishes cruelty by the husband 'or his relatives', which includes female relatives such as the mother-in-law or sister-in-law. Courts have, however, cautioned against mechanically implicating all family members.

question: What is the offence when a public servant demands a bribe?
expected_answer: Bribery by public servants is punished under the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988 (as amended in 2018), not the BNS — taking undue advantage to perform a public duty improperly. Complaints go to the Lokayukta/CVC/Anti-Corruption Bureau; giving a bribe is also an offence, with protection if you report being coerced within 7 days.
required_facts: giving a bribe also an offence

question: Someone hacked my phone and is blackmailing me with private photos, demanding money. What should I do first?
expected_answer: Do not pay. Preserve everything (messages, numbers, screenshots), report immediately on the 1930 cyber helpline and cybercrime.gov.in, and file an FIR — extortion under Section 308 BNS plus IT Act offences (66E, 67) apply. Courts can order urgent takedown of the content.

question: Is honour killing treated specially under the BNS?
expected_answer: There is no separate 'honour killing' offence — it is murder under Section 103 BNS (death or life imprisonment), and group killings on caste or community grounds can attract the mob-lynching provision in Section 103(2). Couples facing threats can seek police protection and courts routinely grant it.

question: What are 'general exceptions' in criminal law?
expected_answer: General exceptions are defences that negate criminal liability across all offences — accident, acts of a child under 7, unsoundness of mind, intoxication against one's will, consent in limited cases, acts done in good faith for a person's benefit, and private defence. The accused must establish the exception.
required_facts: private defence and unsoundness of mind are examples

question: Which provision governs FIR registration under the new criminal procedure law?
expected_answer: FIR registration is governed by Section 173 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, which replaced Section 154 CrPC. For cognizable offences, police must register the FIR; information can also be given electronically.

question: What is a Zero FIR?
expected_answer: A Zero FIR is an FIR registered at any police station regardless of where the offence occurred, later transferred to the police station with jurisdiction. The BNSS (Section 173) made this statutory — no police station can refuse a cognizable complaint for lack of jurisdiction.
required_facts: any police station regardless of jurisdiction

question: Can I file an FIR online without going to the police station?
expected_answer: Yes. Under Section 173 BNSS, information about a cognizable offence can be given by electronic communication (e-FIR), which must then be signed within three days to be taken on record. Many states also run online FIR/complaint portals for specified offences.
required_facts: electronic FIR permitted under Section 173 BNSS

question: Am I entitled to a copy of the FIR I filed, and does it cost anything?
expected_answer: Yes. The informant is entitled to a copy of the FIR free of cost, immediately upon registration, under Section 173 BNSS. Victims are also entitled to a free copy of the police report/chargesheet.

question: The police station is refusing to register my FIR for a cognizable offence. What are my remedies?
expected_answer: First, send your complaint in writing to the Superintendent of Police, who can direct registration or investigate personally. If that fails, apply to the Magistrate to order an investigation. You can also file at any other police station as a Zero FIR under Section 173 BNSS. Refusal to register a cognizable FIR is itself misconduct.

question: For minor offences, can police just send me a notice instead of arresting me?
expected_answer: Yes. For offences punishable up to 7 years, arrest is the exception: police issue a notice of appearance under Section 35(3) BNSS (the old Section 41A CrPC). If you comply with the notice, you should not be arrested unless police record reasons why arrest is necessary.
required_facts: arrest is exception if notice complied with

question: I received a police notice under Section 35(3) BNSS. What should I do?
expected_answer: Appear before the officer as directed (or seek a reasonable rescheduling in writing), cooperate with the investigation, and keep proof of compliance. Complying protects you from arrest in most cases; ignoring the notice can justify arrest. Consult a criminal lawyer before attending if the allegation is serious.

question: What rights do I have if I am arrested?
expected_answer: You must be told the grounds of arrest, can inform a relative or friend, must be produced before a Magistrate within 24 hours, have the right to consult a lawyer of your choice, and to free legal aid if you cannot afford one. Medical examination after arrest is mandated, and police must display arrest information.
required_facts: right to lawyer and legal aid

question: What is anticipatory bail and which provision governs it now?
expected_answer: Anticipatory bail is a direction that a person apprehending arrest for a non-bailable offence be released on bail in the event of arrest. It is governed by Section 482 BNSS (formerly Section 438 CrPC), sought from the Sessions Court or High Court.

question: How long can an undertrial prisoner be kept in jail before they must be released on bail?
expected_answer: Under Section 479 BNSS, an undertrial (in offences not punishable with death or life imprisonment) must be released on bail after detention of half the maximum sentence for the offence. A first-time offender must be released on bond after one-third. The jail superintendent has a duty to apply for eligible prisoners.

question: My brother, never convicted before, has spent 14 months in jail as an undertrial for an offence with a maximum sentence of 3 years. Can he get out?
expected_answer: Yes. As a first-time offender he became entitled to release on bond after serving one-third of the maximum (12 months) under Section 479 BNSS. The jail superintendent is duty-bound to move the court; a bail application citing Section 479 should succeed. Contact the DLSA for free legal aid.
required_facts: one-third of maximum for first-time offender

question: Within how many days must charges be framed after the first hearing?
expected_answer: Under Section 251 BNSS, the charge must be framed within 60 days from the date of first hearing on the charge. Charges can also be framed through audio-video means.

question: How soon must a court deliver judgment after a criminal trial ends?
expected_answer: Under Section 258 BNSS, judgment must be delivered within 30 days of completion of arguments, extendable to 45 days for recorded reasons.

question: As a victim, am I entitled to know what is happening in the police investigation?
expected_answer: Yes. Under Section 193(3) BNSS, police must inform the informant/victim of the progress of the investigation within 90 days, including by electronic means. Victims also get a free copy of the chargesheet.

question: Are police required to video-record searches of my house?
expected_answer: Yes. Section 105 BNSS makes audio-video recording of search and seizure mandatory, preferably by mobile phone, and the recording must be forwarded to the Magistrate. This is a key safeguard against planted evidence.
required_facts: videography of search and seizure mandatory

question: Who can claim maintenance under Section 144 BNSS?
expected_answer: A wife unable to maintain herself, minor children (legitimate or illegitimate), adult children unable to maintain themselves due to abnormality or injury, and parents unable to maintain themselves can claim monthly maintenance from a person with sufficient means under Section 144 BNSS (formerly Section 125 CrPC).

question: My elderly parents' son refuses to support them. Do they have a quick legal remedy?
expected_answer: Yes. Parents unable to maintain themselves can seek monthly maintenance from a child with sufficient means under Section 144 BNSS before the Magistrate — a summary, low-cost remedy. The Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act, 2007 provides an even faster Tribunal route with monthly maintenance and possible eviction of neglectful children from the parents' home.

question: What is the difference between bail, anticipatory bail and interim bail?
expected_answer: Regular bail is release from custody after arrest, granted by the court trying the case. Anticipatory bail (Section 482 BNSS) is protection sought before arrest from the Sessions Court or High Court. Interim bail is short-term release pending decision of the main bail application.

question: Police want to question me but I fear arrest in a false case. What can I do in advance?
expected_answer: Apply for anticipatory bail under Section 482 BNSS in the Sessions Court (or High Court) with facts showing the case is false and you will cooperate. If granted, police must release you on bail upon any arrest. Separately, for offences up to 7 years you should normally get a Section 35(3) notice rather than be arrested.

question: Within what time must police complete investigation and file the chargesheet?
expected_answer: There is no absolute limit for filing the chargesheet, but if it is not filed within 60 days (offences punishable under 10 years) or 90 days (graver offences) of first remand, the accused becomes entitled to default bail. Investigations into offences against women and children have special timelines — rape investigation within 2 months.
required_facts: default bail after 60 or 90 days without chargesheet

question: What is 'default bail'?
expected_answer: Default bail is the indefeasible right of an arrested person to be released on bail when police fail to complete investigation and file the chargesheet within the statutory period after remand (typically 60 or 90 days depending on the offence).
required_facts: right arises from failure to file chargesheet in time

question: How long can police keep me in custody before producing me in court?
expected_answer: An arrested person must be produced before a Magistrate within 24 hours of arrest, excluding journey time — a constitutional guarantee under Article 22(2) as well. Detention beyond that without a Magistrate's order is illegal.

question: What is a chargesheet?
expected_answer: A chargesheet (police report under Section 193 BNSS) is the final report police file in court after investigation, listing the accused, the evidence collected, witnesses and the offences made out. The court takes cognizance on its basis; if evidence is insufficient, police file a closure report instead.

question: What is the difference between a summons case and a warrant case?
expected_answer: A warrant case relates to offences punishable with death, life imprisonment or more than 2 years; a summons case covers lighter offences. Warrant cases follow a fuller trial procedure with formal charge framing; summons cases follow a simpler, faster procedure.
required_facts: warrant case for offences above 2 years

question: Can a court try an absconding accused in his absence?
expected_answer: Yes — a significant BNSS innovation. A proclaimed offender who absconds to evade trial can now be tried and even convicted in absentia, after the court follows the prescribed safeguards. Earlier, trials simply stalled until the accused was traced.
required_facts: trial in absentia of proclaimed offenders permitted under BNSS

question: Do all criminal cases require me to hire a lawyer, or will the state provide one?
expected_answer: If you cannot afford a lawyer, you are entitled to free legal aid — a right under Article 39A, the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987 and criminal procedure. Ask the court or the District Legal Services Authority (DLSA); legal aid counsel is provided at state expense, including at the remand stage.

question: The police took my phone during a search. Do they have to give me any record of it?
expected_answer: Yes. Seizure requires a seizure memo listing the items, signed by witnesses, with a copy to you. Under Section 105 BNSS the search and seizure must also be video-recorded and the recording sent to the Magistrate. You can apply to the court for release of seized items needed for daily use.

question: What is remand — police custody versus judicial custody?
expected_answer: After arrest, the Magistrate decides custody: police custody means detention with police for interrogation (strictly capped in the initial period); judicial custody means jail under court authority. Police custody is the exception and total detention without chargesheet beyond 60/90 days triggers default bail.

question: Can a woman be called to the police station for questioning at night?
expected_answer: A woman cannot be required to attend the police station for questioning — she is to be questioned at her residence in the presence of family/witnesses. Arrest of a woman after sunset and before sunrise is barred except in exceptional circumstances with prior permission of a Magistrate, and only by a woman officer.
required_facts: no arrest of woman after sunset without Magistrate permission

question: Who records the statement of a rape survivor and where?
expected_answer: The statement is to be recorded by a woman police officer, at the survivor's residence or a place of her choice, preferably in the presence of family or a social worker, and can be audio-video recorded. The Magistrate also records her statement promptly; identity disclosure is prohibited.
required_facts: residence or place of her choice

question: What happens after I file a private complaint before a Magistrate instead of an FIR?
expected_answer: The Magistrate examines you and your witnesses on oath, may order an inquiry or police investigation, and if a prima facie case exists, issues process (summons/warrant) to the accused. If not, the complaint is dismissed with reasons. This route suits cases where police decline action.
required_facts: Magistrate may order investigation or issue process

question: What is a 'proclaimed offender'?
expected_answer: A person against whom a warrant is pending who absconds is proclaimed by the court to appear; failing to appear makes them a proclaimed offender, whose property can be attached and who can now be tried in absentia under the BNSS. Harbouring them is an offence.

question: The court summoned me as a witness in a criminal case. Do I have to go?
expected_answer: Yes. A witness summons is legally binding — unjustified absence can lead to a bailable warrant and even prosecution. Witnesses are entitled to expenses, and many states have witness protection schemes; courts increasingly allow evidence by video-conferencing.

question: What does 'taking cognizance' mean?
expected_answer: Taking cognizance is the judicial act by which a Magistrate applies their mind to an offence — on a police report, a private complaint, or their own knowledge — and decides to proceed. It marks the start of the court's role in the case.
required_facts: Magistrate applies mind to offence and proceeds

question: Can criminal proceedings against me be quashed if the dispute is settled?
expected_answer: Compoundable offences can be settled directly. For others (like cheating or matrimonial cases), the High Court can quash the FIR or proceedings on genuine settlement using its inherent powers, if the offence is primarily personal and no public interest suffers. Heinous offences are generally not quashed on settlement.
required_facts: High Court inherent power to quash

question: What is plea bargaining and when can I use it?
expected_answer: Plea bargaining lets an accused plead guilty in exchange for a reduced sentence, for offences punishable up to 7 years — excluding offences against women or children under 14 and socio-economic offences. The application is made to the court, followed by a mutually satisfactory disposition including victim compensation.
required_facts: excludes offences against women and children

question: My FIR was closed by police with a closure report. Is that the end?
expected_answer: No. The Magistrate must give the informant notice before accepting a closure report, and you can file a protest petition. The Magistrate can reject the closure, order further investigation, or take cognizance and proceed. You can also pursue a private complaint.

question: Are handcuffs routinely allowed on arrested persons?
expected_answer: No. Handcuffing is not routine — the BNSS permits it only for specified categories (habitual/repeat offenders, or those accused of grave offences like terrorism, organised crime, murder, rape), and courts continue to treat unjustified handcuffing as a violation of dignity under Article 21.

question: What is the punishment procedure when the accused is dead, insane, or a company?
expected_answer: Proceedings abate on the accused's death (except some property proceedings). An accused of unsound mind incapable of defence has the trial postponed with treatment safeguards. Companies are prosecuted through representatives and punished with fines since they cannot be jailed.

question: How do I get my seized vehicle released while the case is pending?
expected_answer: Apply to the court for interim custody (supurdari) of the vehicle on bond, with proof of ownership (RC). The BNSS facilitates quicker disposal of case property — courts photograph/videograph the property and release it, since keeping vehicles rotting in police stations serves no one.
required_facts: release on bond with ownership proof

question: What is a 'non-cognizable report' (NCR) and why does it matter?
expected_answer: For non-cognizable offences (e.g. simple abuse), police record an NCR instead of an FIR and cannot investigate or arrest without a Magistrate's order. If police log your cognizable complaint as a mere NCR to avoid work, escalate to the SP or Magistrate.

question: Is there a time limit for filing criminal complaints?
expected_answer: For offences punishable up to 3 years, limitation applies: 6 months (fine-only), 1 year (up to 1 year imprisonment), 3 years (1-3 years imprisonment), with the court able to condone delay in the interest of justice. Graver offences have no limitation period.
required_facts: limitation only for offences up to 3 years

question: What is Section 163 BNSS (the old Section 144 CrPC) used for?
expected_answer: Section 163 BNSS empowers a Magistrate to issue urgent prohibitory orders — restricting assembly, movement or activities — to prevent danger to life, health or public tranquillity. Note the trap: 'Section 144' in the BNSS is maintenance of family, not prohibitory orders.

question: Police have called me only as a witness. Can they detain me?
expected_answer: No. A witness summoned to give information cannot be detained; males under 15, over 60, women and disabled persons cannot even be required to attend the police station and are to be questioned at their residence. If questioning turns custodial, rights of an arrested person apply.
required_facts: women and seniors questioned at residence

question: What is a 'test identification parade'?
expected_answer: A test identification parade (TIP) has a witness pick out the accused from among similar-looking persons before a Magistrate, to test identification before trial. Refusing to participate can invite an adverse inference; TIP evidence corroborates, but conviction rests on court identification.
required_facts: witness identifies accused among similar persons

question: The accused in my case got bail. Can bail be cancelled?
expected_answer: Yes. Bail can be cancelled if the accused threatens witnesses, tampers with evidence, commits another offence, or violates bail conditions. Apply to the court that granted bail (or a higher court) with specific instances; courts cancel bail sparingly but do so on proof of misuse.
required_facts: cancellation for threatening witnesses or violating conditions

question: What are my options if I am convicted — how do appeals work?
expected_answer: A conviction by a Magistrate is appealable to the Sessions Court; Sessions convictions go to the High Court, and onward to the Supreme Court in limited cases. Appeals must be filed within the limitation period (with condonation possible), and the appellate court can suspend the sentence and grant bail pending appeal.
required_facts: Magistrate to Sessions, Sessions to High Court
sentence can be suspended pending appeal

question: Do the new criminal procedure timelines apply to cases filed before July 2024?
expected_answer: Pending investigations, trials and appeals begun under the CrPC continue under the CrPC; the BNSS applies to proceedings initiated on or after 1 July 2024. Some beneficial provisions like Section 479 undertrial relief have been applied to existing prisoners too, per Supreme Court directions.
required_facts: pending CrPC proceedings continue under CrPC

question: What is a 'summary trial'?
expected_answer: A summary trial is a fast-track procedure for petty offences where the court records evidence in abbreviated form and disposes of the case quickly; the BNSS expanded mandatory summary trials for petty offences and allows it for offences punishable up to 3 years, with a sentence cap of 3 months in summary proceedings.

question: Can courts hear criminal proceedings by video conference?
expected_answer: Yes. The BNSS expressly allows trials, inquiries, recording of evidence and appearances by audio-video electronic means — a major digitisation push. Statements, charge framing and even some appearances of the accused can happen electronically.

question: What is a First Information Report actually supposed to contain?
expected_answer: The FIR records the first information of a cognizable offence: informant details, time/place, the substance of the allegation and persons involved if known. It is read back and signed, a free copy given, and it need not be an encyclopaedia — details can follow in investigation.

question: My complaint is about an offence that happened in another state. Can I still report it here?
expected_answer: Yes. File a Zero FIR at your local police station under Section 173 BNSS — they must register it regardless of jurisdiction and transfer it to the correct police station. Online reporting via state portals or cybercrime.gov.in (for cyber offences) is another route.

question: What safeguards exist for arrest of women and children?
expected_answer: Women: arrest by/with a woman officer, no arrest after sunset without Magistrate's permission, medical exam by/under a woman doctor. Children in conflict with law are not 'arrested' into police lockups — they are apprehended and produced before the Juvenile Justice Board, and cannot be kept in jail.
required_facts: woman officer for arrest of women
children go before Juvenile Justice Board

question: What is 'further investigation' after a chargesheet?
expected_answer: Police can continue investigating even after filing a chargesheet and file supplementary reports when new evidence surfaces. Under the BNSS, further investigation after trial begins requires court permission and is to be completed within 90 days, extendable by the court.
required_facts: 90 days with court permission during trial

question: Someone I know was arrested and the family was not told anything. Is that legal?
expected_answer: No. Police must inform a nominated relative/friend of the arrest and place of detention, record it, and display arrest details at the police station/district headquarters. The arrested person must see a Magistrate within 24 hours. A habeas corpus petition lies if detention is concealed.

question: Is confession to police admissible in court?
expected_answer: No. A confession made to a police officer is inadmissible; only a confession recorded by a Magistrate with due safeguards counts. However, information from the accused leading to discovery of facts (like recovery of a weapon) is admissible to that extent.

question: What is a 'charge' in a criminal trial and why does it matter?
expected_answer: The charge is the precise accusation framed by the court — the offence, time, place and manner — which the accused must answer. Trial proceeds only on framed charges (BNSS requires framing within 60 days of first hearing), and material defects in the charge can vitiate a conviction.

question: Can I withdraw an FIR I filed?
expected_answer: You cannot simply 'withdraw' an FIR — once registered, investigation is with the police. You can give a statement that the matter is resolved; for compoundable offences the case can be compounded, and for others the accused can seek quashing in the High Court based on settlement.

question: What happens at the 'first hearing' if I'm summoned as an accused in a summons case?
expected_answer: The particulars of the offence are put to you (no formal charge in summons cases); you may plead guilty — with the option in petty cases to plead guilty by post/electronically and pay the fine — or claim trial, after which prosecution evidence begins. Engage a lawyer or seek legal aid before the plea.
required_facts: guilty plea by post in petty cases

question: Are mercy petitions part of criminal procedure?
expected_answer: Yes. A convict sentenced to death can petition the Governor (Article 161) and the President (Article 72) for pardon or commutation; the BNSS now prescribes timelines for filing mercy petitions after appeals are exhausted. Courts can review inordinate delay in deciding them.

question: What is the Directorate of Prosecution?
expected_answer: The BNSS mandates a Directorate of Prosecution in every state and district — officers who supervise public prosecutors, monitor cases, and decide on appeals — to professionalise prosecution independent of the police.
required_facts: mandated in every state and district

question: The magistrate offered to send our cheque-bounce-related assault case to mediation. Is that allowed in criminal cases?
expected_answer: For compoundable offences and quasi-criminal matters like cheque bounce, courts routinely refer parties to mediation/Lok Adalat; a settlement leads to compounding or quashing. Serious non-compoundable offences cannot be settled through mediation.
required_facts: mediation for compoundable and cheque-bounce matters

question: When must police forward the FIR to the Magistrate?
expected_answer: Promptly — the FIR must be sent to the Magistrate without delay so the information is on judicial record early. Unexplained delay in dispatch invites suspicion of ante-timing and can weaken the prosecution case.
required_facts: FIR forwarded to Magistrate without delay

question: What is a preliminary enquiry before FIR registration, and when is it allowed?
expected_answer: Under Section 173(3) BNSS, for cognizable offences punishable between 3 and 7 years, an officer may — with prior permission — hold a preliminary enquiry within 14 days to check whether a prima facie case exists before registering the FIR. For other cognizable offences, immediate registration remains the rule.

question: Are forensic experts now required at crime scenes?
expected_answer: Yes. The BNSS makes forensic expert visits to the crime scene mandatory for offences punishable with 7 years or more, with videography of the process — a push toward evidence-based investigation.
required_facts: mandatory forensics for offences punishable 7 years or more

question: I gave my statement to police. Do I sign it?
expected_answer: No — statements to police during investigation are not signed by the maker. They can be used mainly to contradict a witness at trial, not as substantive evidence. Statements to a Magistrate are different: recorded on oath and signed.

question: When did the BNSS replace the CrPC, and what is its full name?
expected_answer: The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 replaced the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 with effect from 1 July 2024.

question: Can police search my house without a warrant?
expected_answer: Generally a search needs a warrant, but police can search without one during investigation of a cognizable offence when obtaining a warrant would cause undue delay — after recording reasons. Two independent witnesses must attest the search, Section 105 BNSS requires audio-video recording, and you are entitled to a copy of the seizure memo.
required_facts: warrantless search only with recorded reasons

question: Can police arrest me for a non-cognizable offence like simple defamation?
expected_answer: Not without a warrant or Magistrate's order — for non-cognizable offences police cannot arrest or even investigate on their own; the complainant must approach the Magistrate. Arrest powers without warrant exist only for cognizable offences, and even there Section 35 BNSS conditions apply.
required_facts: no warrantless arrest for non-cognizable offences

question: As the victim, can I have my own lawyer participate in the criminal trial alongside the public prosecutor?
expected_answer: Yes. The victim can engage an advocate to assist the prosecution (with the court's permission the advocate can act meaningfully, including suggesting questions); victims also have rights to be heard at key stages — bail hearings in serious offences, withdrawal of prosecution, and compensation — and to appeal against acquittal in specified cases.
required_facts: right to be heard and appeal

question: Which law governs evidence in Indian courts now?
expected_answer: The Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) replaced the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 with effect from 1 July 2024. It governs what evidence is admissible in civil and criminal courts.

question: Are WhatsApp chats admissible as evidence in court?
expected_answer: Yes. Electronic records including WhatsApp chats, emails and server logs are documents under the BSA and admissible — when produced as copies/printouts, they need a certificate under Section 63(4) BSA (the successor of Section 65B Evidence Act) authenticating the device and process.
forbidden_facts: Section 65B Evidence Act as current law

question: What replaced the Section 65B certificate for electronic evidence?
expected_answer: Section 63 BSA replaced Section 65B of the Evidence Act. The certificate under Section 63(4) accompanies electronic records produced in evidence and is now to be signed both by the person in charge of the device/computer and an expert.

question: I have CCTV footage of the theft at my shop. How do I make it usable in court?
expected_answer: Preserve the original DVR/storage untouched, give police a copy with the exact date/time and camera details, and furnish a Section 63(4) BSA certificate describing the device and copying process. Hand over the original if seized under a proper memo — chain of custody matters.

question: What is a dying declaration and is it enough to convict someone?
expected_answer: A dying declaration is a statement by a person about the cause of their death or its circumstances, admissible under Section 26 BSA even though the maker cannot be cross-examined. If found voluntary and reliable, it alone can sustain a conviction — corroboration is a rule of prudence, not law.
required_facts: can alone sustain conviction if reliable

question: Is a confession made to a police officer valid evidence?
expected_answer: No. Confessions to police officers are inadmissible under Section 23 BSA, as are confessions in police custody unless made before a Magistrate. Only the part of custodial information that distinctly leads to discovery of a fact (e.g. recovery of the weapon) is provable.

question: Who has to prove guilt in a criminal case — the accused or the state?
expected_answer: The prosecution must prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt; the accused is presumed innocent and generally need only raise a reasonable doubt. Specific statutes create limited reverse burdens (e.g. dowry death presumption, NDPS), where the accused must rebut a presumption.

question: What is the presumption in dowry death cases?
expected_answer: Where a woman dies unnaturally within 7 years of marriage and is shown to have been harassed for dowry soon before death, the court shall presume the husband/relative caused the dowry death — shifting the burden to the accused to rebut it. This presumption continues under the BSA.

question: What is the difference between primary and secondary evidence?
expected_answer: Primary evidence is the original document itself; secondary evidence is a substitute — copies, oral accounts of contents — admissible only when the original is unavailable for reasons the law recognises. The BSA treats electronic records as documents, and properly certified electronic outputs are admissible.

question: Can a child testify as a witness?
expected_answer: Yes. Every person is competent to testify if they can understand and rationally answer questions — there is no minimum age. The court tests the child's understanding; a child's evidence, if found reliable after careful scrutiny, can support a conviction.

question: What does 'hostile witness' mean?
expected_answer: A hostile witness is one who resiles from their earlier statement and testifies against the party that called them. With the court's permission that party may cross-examine them. Their evidence is not wiped out — the reliable parts can still be used.

question: My only evidence is circumstantial. Can that convict the accused?
expected_answer: Yes, if the chain of circumstances is complete: each circumstance proved, consistent only with guilt, and excluding every reasonable hypothesis of innocence. Courts convict on circumstantial evidence regularly, but the standard is strict.

question: Are call detail records (CDRs) admissible evidence?
expected_answer: Yes. CDRs are electronic records admissible under Section 63 BSA with the required certificate from the telecom provider's responsible officer. They prove call events and tower location, not the content of conversations.

question: Is expert opinion binding on the court?
expected_answer: No. Opinions of experts (fingerprints, handwriting, DNA, ballistics, digital forensics) are relevant and admissible but only advisory — the court weighs them with other evidence. DNA and fingerprint evidence carry high weight in practice.
required_facts: expert opinion relevant but not binding

question: Can my spouse be forced to testify against me?
expected_answer: Communications during marriage are privileged — a spouse cannot disclose them without the other's consent, except in litigation between the spouses or prosecutions for offences against each other. The spouse may otherwise testify about facts they observed.

question: Are conversations with my lawyer protected?
expected_answer: Yes. Professional communications between lawyer and client are privileged — the lawyer cannot disclose them without consent, and legal advice documents are protected. The privilege does not cover communications made to further a crime or fraud.

question: What is an 'admission' versus a 'confession'?
expected_answer: An admission is a statement suggesting an inference about a fact in issue, made by a party — used in civil and criminal cases. A confession is a species of admission by an accused acknowledging guilt. Confessions face stricter admissibility rules (bar on police confessions).

question: The accused's lawyer says my screenshot is fabricated. How does the court decide?
expected_answer: The court weighs authenticity: the Section 63(4) BSA certificate, metadata, the original device (which can be examined by a digital forensics expert), consistency with other evidence, and cross-examination. Produce the original device or account access where possible — screenshots alone carry less weight.

question: Is evidence obtained illegally (say, a recording made without consent) automatically thrown out?
expected_answer: No. India follows the relevancy rule — illegally obtained evidence is not automatically inadmissible if relevant, though courts weigh its reliability and privacy implications (especially after Puttaswamy). Involuntary confessions and privileged material remain barred.
required_facts: illegally obtained evidence not automatically excluded

question: What is 'burden of proof' in a civil case compared to a criminal case?
expected_answer: Civil cases are decided on preponderance of probabilities — whose version is more probable. Criminal cases require proof beyond reasonable doubt against the accused. The same incident can thus fail criminally yet succeed civilly.

question: Can the accused be convicted solely on a co-accused's confession?
expected_answer: No. A co-accused's confession can only be 'taken into consideration' as supporting material — it is weak evidence requiring independent corroboration and cannot alone found a conviction.

question: What weight does an accomplice's testimony carry?
expected_answer: An accomplice (approver) is a competent witness, but prudence requires corroboration in material particulars connecting the accused — courts treat uncorroborated accomplice testimony with suspicion.

question: Do I have to produce the original sale deed, or will a photocopy do?
expected_answer: Produce the original (primary evidence). A photocopy is secondary evidence admissible only after laying foundation — e.g. the original is lost, destroyed, or with the opposite party who fails to produce it after notice. Registered copies from the Sub-Registrar are commonly used with proper proof.

question: What are 'facts in issue' and 'relevant facts'?
expected_answer: Facts in issue are the facts the case turns on — the ingredients of the offence or claim. Relevant facts are other facts the BSA connects to them (motive, preparation, conduct, alibi), which make the facts in issue more or less probable. Only facts in issue and relevant facts may be proved.
required_facts: facts in issue are the disputed ingredients

question: Is motive necessary to prove a crime?
expected_answer: No. Motive is relevant and strengthens a case — especially one based on circumstantial evidence — but absence of proved motive does not defeat direct, credible evidence of the act.

question: What is an alibi, legally speaking?
expected_answer: An alibi is the plea that the accused was elsewhere when the offence occurred, making participation impossible. The accused must prove it with reasonable certainty; a failed alibi does not itself prove guilt but weakens the defence.

question: Will the court believe my witness if he is my relative?
expected_answer: Relationship alone does not discredit a witness — 'interested witness' testimony is scrutinised more carefully but convicts if found truthful and consistent. Courts reject the notion that family members are automatically unreliable, especially in offences occurring within homes.

question: Can the court presume a fact without proof?
expected_answer: Yes, in defined situations: presumptions of fact (court may presume — e.g. possession of stolen goods soon after theft) and presumptions of law (court shall presume — e.g. genuineness of certified copies, dowry-death presumption). Rebuttable presumptions shift the burden to the other side.

question: How is a document executed 30 years ago treated?
expected_answer: Documents 30 years old produced from proper custody enjoy a presumption of genuine execution and attestation — the 'ancient document' rule — so their formal proof is relaxed, though contents can still be contested.

question: What is cross-examination and why does it matter?
expected_answer: Cross-examination is questioning of a witness by the opposite party to test truthfulness, memory and bias, including leading questions. Evidence not subjected to cross-examination when the opportunity existed carries little weight — it is the core fairness mechanism of trial.

question: The eyewitness gave a slightly different account in court than in his police statement. Is his evidence destroyed?
expected_answer: Not necessarily. Minor discrepancies are natural and do not discredit a witness; material contradictions on core facts do. The police statement can be used to contradict him, and the court separates the grain from the chaff.

question: Are Google Maps location history or Aadhaar authentication logs usable in court?
expected_answer: Yes — they are electronic records admissible under Section 63 BSA with a proper certificate from the record-keeper, subject to relevancy and privacy safeguards. Courts assess reliability of the underlying system and chain of custody.

question: What does 'estoppel' mean?
expected_answer: Estoppel prevents a person from denying what they earlier represented, when another person acted on that representation to their detriment — e.g. a landlord who accepted someone as tenant cannot later deny the tenancy's existence to defeat their rights.

question: Does silence of the accused prove guilt?
expected_answer: No. The accused has a constitutional right against self-incrimination (Article 20(3)) and their silence cannot substitute for prosecution proof, though failure to explain incriminating circumstances within their special knowledge can be an additional link in a circumstantial case.

question: What is 'res gestae' or 'part of the same transaction'?
expected_answer: Statements and acts so connected with the incident as to form part of the same transaction — like a spontaneous cry naming the attacker during the assault — are admissible even though otherwise hearsay, because spontaneity leaves no room for fabrication.

question: Is hearsay evidence allowed?
expected_answer: Generally no — a witness must depose to what they personally perceived. Exceptions exist: dying declarations (Section 26 BSA), statements in the course of the same transaction, admissions, and statements of persons who cannot be called (dead/unavailable) in defined situations.

question: My accused brother-in-law's phone had photos of the stolen jewellery. What evidentiary principle applies?
expected_answer: Recent unexplained possession of stolen property lets the court presume the possessor is the thief or receiver. The photos are electronic evidence (Section 63 BSA certificate needed); the recovered jewellery itself should be seized under a memo and identified by the owner.
required_facts: presumption from recent possession of stolen property

question: Can judges use their personal knowledge of facts in deciding a case?
expected_answer: Only through judicial notice of well-established facts (laws, official seals, standard calendars, notorious public facts). For everything else the judge must decide on the evidence on record, not private knowledge.
required_facts: judicial notice limited to established facts

question: What is the evidentiary status of a suicide note?
expected_answer: A genuine suicide note is admissible as a statement about the circumstances of the maker's death (dying declaration principle under Section 26 BSA) and can support charges like abetment of suicide — after proof of handwriting/authorship and scrutiny of voluntariness.

question: Bank statements were produced against me without anyone from the bank testifying. Valid?
expected_answer: Bankers' book entries enjoy special treatment: certified copies of bank records are admissible without producing the original ledgers or the banker, under the Bankers' Books Evidence Act read with the BSA's electronic records regime (Section 63 certificate for electronic statements).

question: पुलिस मेरी FIR दर्ज नहीं कर रही है। मुझे क्या करना चाहिए?
expected_answer: संज्ञेय अपराध में FIR दर्ज करना पुलिस का कर्तव्य है (धारा 173 BNSS)। मना करने पर लिखित शिकायत पुलिस अधीक्षक (SP) को भेजें, फिर भी दर्ज न हो तो मजिस्ट्रेट के समक्ष आवेदन करें। आप किसी भी थाने में Zero FIR भी दर्ज करा सकते हैं।

question: पत्नी और बच्चों के भरण-पोषण के लिए कौन सी धारा है?
expected_answer: BNSS की धारा 144 (पुरानी CrPC धारा 125) — पत्नी, बच्चे और माता-पिता मजिस्ट्रेट से मासिक भरण-पोषण का आदेश ले सकते हैं। घरेलू हिंसा अधिनियम की धारा 20 के तहत भी आर्थिक राहत मिलती है।
forbidden_facts: धारा 125 CrPC वर्तमान कानून के रूप में

question: Police FIR nahi likh rahi, bol rahe hain 'civil matter hai'. Kya karu?
expected_answer: Agar cognizable offence hai (jaise cheating, chori, maar-peet) toh FIR register karna police ki duty hai — Section 173 BNSS. Written complaint SP ko bhejo; phir bhi nahi hui toh Magistrate ke paas application do. Kisi bhi thane mein Zero FIR bhi karwa sakte ho. Sach mein pure civil dispute (jaise sirf paise ka lena-dena bina dhokhe ke) mein FIR nahi hoti — wahan civil court jana hoga.

question: Anticipatory bail kya hoti hai aur kab leni chahiye?
expected_answer: Agar lagta hai ki kisi non-bailable case mein aapki arrest ho sakti hai, toh pehle se Sessions Court ya High Court se anticipatory bail le sakte ho — Section 482 BNSS (pehle 438 CrPC). Grant hone par arrest hote hi bail par release karna hota hai. False case ka dar ho toh jaldi lawyer se milkar apply karo.

question: Zero FIR ka matlab kya hai?
expected_answer: Zero FIR wo FIR hai jo kisi bhi police station mein file ho sakti hai, chahe crime kahin aur hua ho — number '0' se register hoti hai aur baad mein sahi jurisdiction wale thane transfer hoti hai. BNSS Section 173 ne ise statutory bana diya hai. Emergency mein bahut kaam aati hai.
